units.title: Can and cannot
units.goal: Say what you are able to do — and refuse something without sounding rude.
explain: 수 is a noun meaning a way, a means. So (으)ㄹ 수 있어요 is literally there is a way to do it, and (으)ㄹ 수 없어요 is there is no way. Vowel stem takes ㄹ 수, consonant stem takes 을 수.

못 in front of the verb says the same thing in one syllable — 못 가요, I can't go. The two are interchangeable most of the time, but 못 puts the blame on circumstances, while (으)ㄹ 수 없다 is flatter and more formal. On a form or a notice you will see the long one.
This pattern is how you say no at work without a flat refusal. 오늘은 잔업 할 수 없어요 states an inability; 오늘은 잔업 안 해요 states a decision. The first is heard as a reason, the second as a stance.

examples.en: I can speak a little Korean.
I can drive a forklift.

examples.ko: 허리가 아파서 무거운 것을 들 수 없어요.
examples.en: My back hurts, so I can't lift heavy things.
I can't do overtime today.

examples.ko: 이 서류는 혼자 쓸 수 없어요.
examples.en: I can't fill in this form on my own.

notes: 잘 하다 is a different idea — doing something well, not being able to do it at all. 한국어를 잘 못해요 means I'm not good at Korean, which is softer and more honest than 한국어를 할 수 없어요.
못 attaches to 하다 verbs the same way 안 does: 일 못 해요, not 못 일해요.

exercises.why: 하다 stem 운전하 ends in a vowel, so ㄹ 수 있어요.
들다 ends in ㄹ, and the ㄹ carries straight into 수.

exercises.ko: 허리가 아파서 무거운 것을 들 수 없어요.
options: My back hurts so I can't lift heavy things.
My back hurts when I lift heavy things.
Lifting heavy things is my job.

exercises.q: Your Korean is basic and you want to say so modestly. Which is best?
exercises.why: 잘 못해요 says not very good at it. 할 수 없어요 claims you cannot speak it at all.

pairs.bEn: I can speak Korean.
pairs.note: ㄹ 수 있다 is literally there is a way to do it. The 수 is a noun, which is why 있다/없다 follows it.

pairs.bEn: I can't do it.
pairs.note: The negative swaps 있다 for 없다 — you never say 안 할 수 있어요. In speech you will also hear 못 해요, which is blunter.

pairs.bEn: I can't go tomorrow.
pairs.note: The same meaning. 못 is short and spoken. (으)ㄹ 수 없다 is flatter and more formal, and it is the one you will read on forms and notices.

pairs.bEn: I'm not very good at Korean.
pairs.note: 잘 turns cannot into not good at. It is the honest answer when you speak some Korean, and the polite one.

units.title: Must, and must not
units.goal: Read a safety rule and understand exactly what it requires of you.
explain: 아/어야 되다 is have to. Build the 아/어 form, then add 야 되다: 가야 돼요 I have to go, 써야 돼요 I have to wear it. 하다 gives 해야 돼요.
(으)면 안 되다 is must not. Literally if you do it, it does not become — Korean states a prohibition as a consequence rather than a command. 들어가면 안 돼요, you must not go in.
되다 and 하다 are both used here — 해야 돼요 and 해야 해요 mean the same thing. 돼요 is the spoken default; 해요 turns up more in writing. On safety notices you will usually meet the formal 해야 합니다 and 하면 안 됩니다.

examples.en: You have to wear safety shoes in the work area.

examples.ko: 기계를 만지기 전에 전원을 꺼야 돼요.
examples.en: You have to switch the power off before touching the machine.
You must not smoke here.
You must not go without a helmet on.
You don't have to come in tomorrow.

notes: 아/어도 돼요? is how you ask permission: 화장실 가도 돼요? — may I go to the toilet? The answer is 네, 돼요 or 아니요, 안 돼요.
안 하면 안 돼요 is a double negative that means you must do it. It is common and it is not a mistake — read it as it won't do if you don't.

exercises.qEn: You have to wear safety shoes in the work area.
exercises.why: 아/어야 되다 is the obligation pattern.

exercises.qEn: May I go to the toilet?

exercises.ko: 기계를 만지기 전에 전원을 꺼야 돼요.
options: Switch the power off before touching the machine.
Touch the machine before switching it on.
The power is off, so touch the machine.

exercises.q: A sign reads 안전모를 착용해야 합니다. What does it require?
exercises.why: 착용하다 is to wear or put on; 해야 합니다 is the formal must.

pairs.bEn: I have to wear safety shoes.
pairs.note: 아/어야 되다 is obligation. It is all over a workplace, on every sign and in every instruction.

pairs.bEn: You must not smoke here.
pairs.note: 면 안 되다 is the prohibition. Literally: if you do it, it won't do. This is the exact phrasing a supervisor will use.

pairs.aEn: You can go home before the others.
pairs.bEn: You must not go home before the others.
pairs.note: 아/어도 돼요 gives permission. (으)면 안 돼요 takes it away. Listen for 도 or 면 — the rest of the sentence is the same.

pairs.bEn: You have to wear gloves.
pairs.note: One extra 안 turns the rule upside down. 안 하면 안 돼요 means it won't do if you don't, so you must.

units.title: If, and when
units.goal: Set a condition — for a request, a warning, or a plan.
explain: (으)면 covers both if and whenever. Vowel stem takes 면, consonant stem takes 으면. Korean does not separate the two meanings the way English does, and the difference almost never matters in practice.
The clause with 면 always comes first. 시간이 있으면 도와주세요 — if you have time, please help. Reversing them is not an option in Korean word order.

면 is also the polite way to make a request into a suggestion, which is its real value at work. 괜찮으면 내일 이야기해도 돼요? — if it's all right, could we talk tomorrow? You have asked for something without demanding it.

examples.en: If you have time, please help me.
If you're ill, go to the hospital.
If you press this button, the machine stops.
What do I do if my wages don't come in?
If you study Korean every day, you improve.

notes: 만약 or 혹시 in front flags the if clearly — 만약 늦으면, if by any chance I'm late. Neither is necessary; both make the condition sound more hypothetical.
Do not confuse 면 with 서. 아파서 쉬어요 means I'm resting because I'm ill — a real reason. 아프면 쉬어요 means when I'm ill, I rest — a rule.

exercises.qEn: If you have time, please help me.
exercises.why: 있 ends in a consonant, so 으면.

exercises.qEn: If you're ill, go to the hospital.
exercises.why: 면 sets the condition. 아파서 would state it as a fact that already happened.

exercises.qEn: If you press this button, the machine stops.

options: What do I do if my wages don't come in?
My wages came in, what now?

exercises.q: Which sentence gives a reason rather than a condition?
exercises.why: 아/어서 states a cause that is actually the case.

pairs.bEn: If it rains, use an umbrella.
pairs.note: 면 welds the condition onto the front of the sentence, and the two halves become one thought instead of two.

pairs.bEn: Don't come if you don't have time.
pairs.note: 면 attaches after 으 when the stem ends in a consonant — the same 으 you met in 으세요.

pairs.bEn: I'm resting because I'm tired.
pairs.note: 면 sets a condition: whenever that is true. 아/어서 gives a reason that is true right now.

pairs.bEn: If work has finished, call me.
pairs.note: Put the past inside 면 and the condition is about something already done. The first waits for the end of work; the second asks if it has ended.

units.title: Before, after, and while
units.goal: Order the events of a shift, and describe a procedure in the right sequence.
explain: 기 전에 is before. It goes on the plain stem and never changes: 밥을 먹기 전에, before eating. 전 on its own also works after a time word — 3년 전에, three years ago.
(으)ㄴ 후에 is after. It needs the past-modifier shape: vowel stem takes ㄴ 후에, consonant stem takes 은 후에. 먹은 후에, after eating. 다음에 and 뒤에 are used the same way.

(으)ㄹ 때 is when or while, covering a stretch of time rather than a point: 일할 때 while working, 한국에 처음 왔을 때 when I first came to Korea. Note that the past goes on 때, not in the main clause — 왔을 때, not 왔을 때예요.

examples.en: I stretch before work.
Clean it after switching the machine off.
I always wear gloves when working.

examples.ko: 한국에 처음 왔을 때 아무것도 몰랐어요.
examples.en: When I first came to Korea, I knew nothing.

examples.ko: 다치면 바로 반장님한테 말하세요. 참지 마세요.
examples.en: If you get hurt, tell the team leader right away. Don't put up with it.

notes: Only 기 전에 uses the plain stem. Both of the others need a modifier shape, which is the topic of unit 20 — if the endings look arbitrary now, they will not after that unit.
때 attaches straight to a noun with no particle: 점심 때, 휴가 때, 방학 때.

exercises.why: 기 전에 attaches to the plain stem and means before.

exercises.qEn: Clean it after switching the machine off.
exercises.why: 후에 needs the past modifier: 끄다 → 끈.

exercises.qEn: I always wear gloves when working.

exercises.ko: 한국에 처음 왔을 때 아무것도 몰랐어요.
options: When I first came to Korea I knew nothing.
I want to go to Korea for the first time.

exercises.why: 때 attaches straight to a noun with nothing between.

pairs.aEn: Wash your hands before you eat.
pairs.bEn: Take the medicine after you eat.
pairs.note: Before takes 기 전에 on the plain stem. After takes 은/ㄴ 후에, which is a past modifier — the eating is already done.

pairs.bEn: I was careful when I was working.
pairs.note: ㄹ 때 is while or when. Put the tense inside it — 했을 때 — and you are talking about a particular past occasion.

pairs.aEn: Clean it before you switch the machine off.
pairs.bEn: Clean it after you switch the machine off.
pairs.note: Only the time word changed, and the order of the two actions is reversed. 기 전에 goes on the plain stem; 후에 needs the ㄴ shape.

pairs.bEn: Let's meet before lunch.
pairs.note: After a noun, 때 is during it and 전에 is before it. Neither needs anything between it and the noun.

units.title: Setting the scene before you ask
units.goal: Say the background first — the way Korean conversations actually open.
explain: 는데 is the most-used ending in spoken Korean and the hardest to translate, because it does not mean any one thing. It puts a piece of background on the table so the next sentence has somewhere to land.

Three jobs. Background: 지금 바쁜데 이따 이야기해요 — I'm busy right now, so let's talk later. Contrast: 한국어는 어려운데 재미있어요 — Korean is hard but it's interesting. And a soft opening that trails off, where the request is left unsaid: 저기, 부탁이 있는데요 — er, I have a favour to ask.
The shape depends on what it attaches to. Action verbs take 는데. Descriptive verbs take (으)ㄴ데. Nouns take 인데. The past, for everything, is 았/었는데.

examples.ko: 지금 좀 바쁜데 이따가 이야기해도 돼요?
examples.en: I'm a bit busy now — could we talk later?
Korean is hard, but it's interesting.
Er, I have a favour to ask…

examples.ko: 어제 병원에 갔는데 의사가 쉬라고 했어요.
examples.en: I went to the hospital yesterday, and the doctor told me to rest.
I got my payslip, and the hours look wrong.

examples.ko: 일한 시간이 기록이랑 달라요. 한번 봐 주시겠어요?
examples.en: The hours worked don't match my record. Could you take a look?

notes: 는데요 ending a sentence on its own is an invitation for the other person to respond. It is the Korean equivalent of leaving a sentence hanging, and it is polite rather than rude.
Do not confuse 는데 with 는 데. Written apart, 데 is a place: 아픈 데가 어디예요? — where does it hurt?

exercises.qEn: I'm a bit busy now — could we talk later?
I went to the hospital yesterday, and…
exercises.why: The past takes 았/었는데 whatever the verb type.

exercises.qEn: Korean is hard, but it's interesting.

options: They got the payslip and the hours look wrong.
They want to work more hours.

exercises.q: What does 아픈 데가 어디예요? ask?
exercises.why: Written with a space, 데 is a place — the spot that hurts.

pairs.aEn: I have no time. Please help.
pairs.bEn: I'm short of time — could you help me a moment?
pairs.note: 는데 lays the ground before the ask. Without it the request lands on the listener with no run-up, which is why the first version sounds abrupt.

pairs.bEn: This is good — have a look.
pairs.note: 는데 is not but. It is the setup, and what follows can be a contrast, a request, or just the rest of the story.

pairs.aEn: I have a favour to ask.
pairs.bEn: Er, I have a favour to ask…
pairs.note: 는데요 leaves the sentence open and lets the other person answer first. It is the gentle way to start a request.

pairs.aEn: I'm a bit busy now, so let's talk later.
pairs.bEn: — not Korean.
pairs.note: 바쁘다 describes, so it takes ㄴ데: 바쁜데. 는데 is for action verbs and for 있다 and 없다.

units.title: The formal register
units.goal: Speak the way an office, an interview or a 고용노동부 phone call expects you to.
explain: Everything so far has been the 해요 level — polite, warm, right for almost every situation. Above it sits the 합니다 level: consonant stem takes 습니다, vowel stem takes ㅂ니다. Questions end 습니까 or ㅂ니까.

This is not more polite so much as more public. You use it in an interview, on the phone to an office, in a written statement, in an announcement, and when a soldier or a shop's loudspeaker addresses you. 감사합니다 and 죄송합니다 are this level, which is why they sound weightier than 고마워요 and 미안해요.

(으)시 is a separate dial, and it turns instead on who you are talking about. Slot it into the verb when the subject is someone senior: 사장님이 오십니다, the director is coming. You never use it about yourself. Combine the two dials freely — 오세요 is 해요 level with respect, 오십니다 is 합니다 level with respect.

examples.en: Good day. My name is Nguyen Van Nam.
It has been two years since I came to Korea.
I will work diligently.
The director is not in at the moment.
I would be grateful if you could check.

notes: 께서 is the respectful replacement for 이/가, and 께 replaces 에게/한테. You will meet them in writing far more than in speech.
Mixing levels inside one conversation is normal and not an error. Koreans open formally and slide into 해요 as the conversation settles.
겠 inserted before 습니다 adds intention or a softened guess: 하겠습니다 I will do it, 알겠습니다 understood. In an interview, 열심히 하겠습니다 is the expected closing line.

exercises.qEn: My name is Nguyen Van Nam. (formal)
exercises.why: 이다 becomes 입니다 at the 합니다 level.
먹 ends in a consonant, so 습니다.

options: The director is not in at the moment.
I am not in the office.

exercises.q: Which would you use about yourself?

pairs.bEn: I work.
pairs.note: Identical meaning, different register. 합니다 is what you use on the phone to an office, in an interview, and what the exam paper is written in throughout.

pairs.bEn: The boss is coming.
pairs.note: 시 honours the person doing the action, not the person you are speaking to. You never use it about yourself.

pairs.aEn: I have handed in the documents.
pairs.bEn: Have you handed in the documents?
pairs.note: At this level a statement ends in 다 and a question in 까. You will hear 습니까 at every office counter.

pairs.bEn: I work hard.
pairs.note: 겠 adds intention. The first is a promise about the future, the line people close an interview with. The second only describes you.
